LEDE: DT-FBSDE normally fits each stage's value function from the current batch alone and then discards it. This sweep keeps each stage's least-squares normal equations from one iteration to the next instead. Each iteration multiplies the kept equations by a forgetting factor ρ before adding its own batch, which is recursive least squares. Everything else is the batch sweep's best 2-D configuration (batch 16, slope matching, mixed exploration, screened line search). The model is the degree-4 monomial polynomial; each setting runs 5 seeds of 30 s, scored on the same 1,024 held-out rollouts as before.
FINDINGS:
• Carrying the normal equations makes DT-FBSDE worse on both problems, in every setting tried. No setting matched the current method's +3.6% median on the pendulum or its +0.3% on the double integrator. Longer memory is generally worse.
  • Without the reset, the damage grows steadily with memory. For ρ = 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 and 0.95, the pendulum medians are +30%, +80%, +121% and +215%, and the double integrator's are +4.3%, +30%, +42% and +55%. At the same time, accepted updates rise from 1.7–3.4% to 6–24% of iterations. More steps are accepted while the policy gets worse.
  • The reset limits the damage but never closes the gap. Its best settings are ρ = 0.5 (pendulum +16%, double integrator +1.4%) and ρ = 0.8 (+19% and +1.8%). Keeping everything since the last acceptance, ρ = 1, is the worst reset variant on both problems (+47% and +36%). These variants accept fewer updates than the current method: 0.2–1.3% of iterations.
  • What this suggests. With batches of 16, DT-FBSDE behaves like stochastic approximation. Each iteration's fit is a fresh, heavily regularized proposal from 8 samples, and the line search filters them. Memory removes both ingredients:
    • Lost prior: with many rows, the data pin down every coefficient, and the ridge's smoothness preference, which an earlier study showed DT-FBSDE depends on, no longer matters.
    • Stale targets: without the reset, kept rows carry targets computed under older policies.
    • Correlated halves: the two double-estimation halves accumulate shared systematic errors, so the protection from greedy-target bias weakens.
    • Fewer varied proposals: with the reset, the fits change little from one iteration to the next, so the line search sees fewer new candidates.
    This is the same mechanism that made deterministic sigma points stall.
  • These explanations are not yet separated. Short diagnostic runs could tell them apart: scale the ridge with the kept rows, use the non-greedy backward target, and log the line search's cost beside the held-out cost.
SETTINGS:
Each setting is a forgetting factor ρ, applied every iteration, optionally combined with a reset.

  • ρ = 0: today's method. Each iteration fits its own batch of 8 samples per half, plus their slopes.
  • ρ > 0: the fit sees roughly the last 1/(1−ρ) batches. That's 2 batches at ρ = 0.5 and 20 at ρ = 0.95. Old rows fade geometrically, and every batch is kept whether or not the line search accepts its update.
  • Reset on acceptance: also clears the kept equations whenever an update is accepted. Targets are computed from the current tables, which only change on acceptance. So between acceptances, every kept target is current, and even ρ = 1 (keep everything since the last acceptance) is exact.
NOTES:
• Gap is the final policy's held-out cost over the grid dynamic-programming optimum, minus one.
  • "Within 5% at end" counts seeds whose final policy is within 5%.
  • "Median time to 5%" is the charged solver time at which a seed first got there. It's "never" unless at least half the seeds did.
  • "Updates accepted" is the share of iterations whose line search accepted a step.
  • Few seeds: with 5 seeds, differences of a point or two between settings are within seed-to-seed noise.
  • Reproducing: bazel run -c opt //examples:value_model_study -- --phase dt --models "poly4:memory=0.9,reset=1", analyzed by tools/analyze_rls_sweep.py.
